note: Reader-facing release notes for returning readers (modules/reading-switches.mjs). Newest first. Plain words, no internals.

notes: Exactly One Pie no longer stops at each new place: the change is said in a small note at the top of the game while the colours cross over and the carry goes on. When the hat moves on, the next carrier fades in under it.

The folio wall has a new shelf: folios from the maker's own worktable at spwashi.com — real pages, collaged, laminated and painted — each with the question it asks and where in the land it stands. Two of them hang beside Exactly One Pie.
Exactly One Pie: it is not always him under the hat. Each carry the hat settles on someone — the porter, a feast clerk, the Genie, now and then a clown — and at a change of scene it may move on.
Clowns love WAP: a pie in the face. Step into one and it gets the pie, square, with a WAP you can hear; the pie on the plate is no smaller. A toggle under the game turns the sound off.

Exactly One Pie, a small game: someone is destined to spill exactly one pie, and a figure in a hat is carrying one up the lanes of Bonk City. Step across the city as it streams at you; hurry and the pie tilts; Boof steadies it if you pass her. Find it under the hat on the home page, or at the desk with @[pie].

A link can set how the story is read for your whole visit: ?edition=winter gives every changing phrase in the book one edition's words, the same for anyone who opens it; ?lens=bone, ?room=lamp, ?binding=slate and ?without=wonders set the rest.
A chapter opened from such a link says so under its title, with Keep as mine and Let go. Nothing a link sets becomes yours unless you keep it.
Other tellings has Copy this telling: a link that opens the chapter with exactly the words you turned to.
At the desk, ?[links] lists everything a link can carry.

The home page's look has moved out of the top bar and into the story: at the folio house by the parcel gate, the binder keeps six covers on pegs. Tap the underlined words in her sentence to change the cover, the lamp and the shutters.
One book, one binding: the cover you choose at the folio house binds every chapter, and a cover chosen in a chapter's Reading nook binds the home page.
Phrases with a faint wavy line are told more than one way. Tap one to hear its next telling; hold it to see every telling as a card, the ones you have not heard yet face down.
Other tellings, in the rail: turn the hour and every phrase rolls to that hour's words while the light walks with it. Back to now, or the book's own words, whenever you like.
Bind the book: Reading nook → Binding has six spines — rag paper, Bonk glass, salt flat, hearth clay, slate & chalk, starfield.
Begin again, beside Continue reading or under the contents: from the top, keeping everything, or a fresh copy whose marks are set aside so you can put them back.
On a wide screen the page and its rail sit together in the middle, with the room around them.

A chapter's address can now set the stage for one visit, in plain words: ?light=dusk (or dawn, morning, noon, afternoon, night, lamp), ?stage=story with p=3 to frame a passage, ?phrases=turn to let phrases turn with the clock, ?at=19:00 to read the words of that hour. Nothing you set in Switches changes.
Frame this and the light table have Copy stage link: the light, the words and the frame you tuned, as a link anyone can open.
The light table has named cues — dawn, morning, noon, afternoon, dusk, night, lamp — beside the sky you can drag.
The trial once called a living page is now plainly named: Phrases turn with the clock.
A light you hold now stays where you put it while you scroll.

Hold the light: at the end of every section, open the light table and drag the sun across a small sky, turn the scene's warmth, glow, ink, grain and edge, or carry the light with you until you set it down. Each scene's motif already leans its light a little: an egg holds amber low, a hat is pencil on paper, a torch keeps the dark close. Tap a wonder and the light leans toward it.

Frame this: set the passage you are reading on a card — story, square or card proportions — with the chapter's name and address, the type size and the light at hand. The controls step back so the screenshot is clean.

At the table: every chapter now ends with a closed page for playing in it — the place, its light, its people and what they want, three hooks, a d6, things worth carrying out, a bracework move, and the page's own dice.

Sayings: the land's makers have rules they live by — first ink stays; glass over, never scrape; chalk is cheaper than oak — and they travel from chapter to chapter. Tap one to keep it; each has a second reading, in the workshop.

A living page, to try (Switches → A living page, or any chapter with ?try=living): a few phrases in every chapter breathe, turning by the minute, the hour or the day — away from wherever you are reading. The marks glint now and then, like grains in soil. Switch it off and every word is the book's own again.

Bracework in the chapters: where the land's makers write in sigils and braces — the council's law, a brace-box, the joiners' marks, the archive's catalogue, the clerk's new form — the page now reads it with the Spw interpreter and draws what it found.
Every chapter ends by naming the wonders it holds; each is a door to its page in your almanac.
Kept wonders in the almanac now offer a plate prompt: the scene in words, ready to paint from.

Every chapter was revised for the land itself: more of what things are made of, what they smell like, who keeps them, and what lives in the wild places — echo-wrens and salt-whales, pane-snails and seam-otters, kilns and needles and bells.

The first time a chapter names a creature, a contrivance or a piece of bracework, it is marked with a dotted line. Tap it to keep it in your almanac; the card says where else it lives, so finding it again somewhere new fills in its entry.

A new page, the Almanac, keeps what you have found — with silhouettes of what is still out there, the drawing of the figure under the hat, and a combining bench where found things become small realms in braces. (Switches → Wonders in the prose turns the marks off.)
At the desk, ?[almanac] counts what you have kept.

Keep an eye out for the figure under the hat. Each time you notice him, in the margins or the story, a small card says so and his drawing gains a line. Nine sightings, nine strokes. (Switches → Sightings turns the cards off; they are still kept.)

The home page answers back: drawers remember what you have found and stamp it, the land riffles before it chooses, the egg turns when you change its reading, new chapters turn to read once you have read them, and the next stone counts down.
At the desk, ?[sightings] shows your drawing so far.
Book Two begins: two new chapters, The Thursday Nobody Kept and Child, Parcel, or Door. The next stone is set Friday 13 November.
Something has come through the warm furrow without a receipt. It is under a hat.
The home page now says what is new, who is in the story, and the story so far for anyone arriving partway.
The ring of berries has a second, inner ring for Book Two, and Book Two's seals begin a new day at dawn gold.
Keep offline now keeps every chapter, however many there are.
Every setting now says what it changed: a small card beside the control, and a brief gold sweep over the part of the page it touched.

X-ray reading is now called Structure mode, and it answers three gestures. Tap a word, sentence or paragraph and it speaks. Hold one and it stays pinned; hold two and the rail says what they share. Brush across a line with a mouse or pen (or a finger, once Brush with a finger is on) and every word lights, thread by thread, then a note says which threads you crossed, how the sweep leans, and which chambers those threads meet in again.
The egg can be seen three ways on the home page — opal, stone, amber — and the material cabinet keeps what you have noticed.
Every mark on a chapter is now a door: tap a motif, a trope, a thread, or a voice's name and a ring of thirteen boonberries lights up wherever it runs through the book. Tap a berry to go there.
At the desk, &[threads] shows the whole weave; &[thread]{motif} or &[motif]{unspent-wish} follows one.

X-ray reading, in Switches: hover a word, a sentence or a paragraph and the structure shows through — the threads a word belongs to, the way a sentence leans, the sign a paragraph sits under. Click to hold it.
The ants have noticed the egg.
A folio wall: pages under glass, the maker's first. New folios stay liquid until a stone day passes, then go clear.
The ants under the berry rows have torches now, and streets; the Genie, it turns out, did good business with them.
Boof works for the land, not for fruit — a slip that had lingered in the copy is mended everywhere it stood.
Page controls are quieter, and on a phone the page runs to the edge. The genre dial folds away until you want it.
The chapters read in shorter beats now: the long walls of text are broken where the story turns, and the longest sentences breathe.
Genre is tunable: under any chapter's title, choose Tune and move the point between fairy tale, absurd reality and low magic. The story follows the blend.
Every chapter now opens with a choice: read it as Boon, Bane or Bone — the fairytale, the reality being left behind, or the notation underneath.
Several chapters were revised to follow the Egg more closely: less bookkeeping, more warmth, more of what can't be named yet.
The last chapter has a new name: The Shell-Shaped Door.
The margins have started to notice something. Keep an eye on them.
The Scriptorium is now your desk: pick up where you left off, search every chapter, keep the book offline, and see when the next chapter lands.
Everything on the desk is a spell you can tap, then type. Press / there and try ?[next].
The four design lenses in the Scriptorium are now named for the forces they exert: inertia, friction, flux, resonance.
Every chapter now ends with its shelf-mates in any library: call numbers to take into the aisles, and a way to find them near you.
A new trial for readers who keep coming back: the grammar, faintly — each part of a chapter shows the sign it enacts.
Lore.Land can live on your home screen now, and keep every chapter for reading offline (see Switches).
When the network is gone, the offline page shows the chapters on your shelf.
Sharing a chapter shows its painting and title.
Chapter One's opening was tightened: the warm furrow arrives sooner.
A reading nook in the rail: coziness, texture, light from daylight to lamplight, and an optional hearth.
Each chapter now ends by turning the page toward the next one, and the contents are one tap from the dock.
Select any line to get a link straight to it.
Nothing you used went away: the rail and summary are as you left them. See Switches in the rail.
